facts.text: Congress created the Treasury Department on September 2, 1789, and named Alexander Hamilton its first Secretary.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: The nation's first war loans were borrowed from France and the Netherlands to help pay for the American Revolution.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: On January 1, 1783, the new nation's public debt totaled $43 million.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: Robert Morris, nicknamed The Financier, ordered the first tally of total government debt, starting annual Treasury reports.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: Debts from the Revolutionary War amounted to about $75 million by January 1, 1791.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: Hamilton's January 1790 report urged the federal government to take over the states' Revolutionary War debts.
facts.source: National Archives, Prologue blog: The Compromise of 1790

facts.text: At a June 20, 1790 dinner hosted by Jefferson, Hamilton and Madison struck a deal tying state debts to the Potomac capital.
facts.source: National Archives, Prologue blog: The Compromise of 1790

facts.text: In 1790 Hamilton estimated the public debt at $77.1 million and called for new federal bonds to cover it.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: Hamilton argued that a national debt, if it is not excessive, will be to us a national blessing.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: In 1793, George Washington said no money matter was more urgent than regularly paying down the public debt.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt
facts.note: Treasury page quotes Washington's 1793 message: 'No pecuniary consideration is more urgent than the regular redemption and discharge of the public debt.' Paraphrased.

facts.text: Benjamin Franklin is credited with the line: 'Rather go to bed without dinner than to rise in debt.'
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Understanding the National Debt

facts.text: Treasury Secretary Albert Gallatin, the longest-serving in history, made paying down the public debt his priority.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: The War of 1812 pushed the public debt from $45.2 million in January 1812 to $119.2 million by September 1815.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: By January 1835, under Andrew Jackson, the U.S. had paid off all its interest-bearing debt, for the first and only time.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: On January 1, 1835, the total public debt stood at just $33,733.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Historical Debt Outstanding
facts.note: Record shows debt_outstanding_amt 33733.05 for 1835-01-01.

facts.text: In 1835, the federal budget surplus of $17.9 million was bigger than the government's total spending that year.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: The Mexican War cost an estimated $64 million, and Congress authorized new debt to pay for it.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: In 1860 the public debt was $64.8 million, barely more than that year's $63.1 million federal budget.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: The national debt passed $1 billion in 1863 and reached about $2.7 billion after the Civil War ended.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: The Civil War cost the nation an estimated $5.2 billion in direct spending.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: The 1862 Legal Tender Act let Treasury issue $150 million in U.S. notes and sell $500 million in bonds for the war.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: At the close of fiscal 1899, the gross federal debt stood at $1.9 billion.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: The Second Liberty Bond Act of September 24, 1917 set an aggregate limit on federal debt, a root of today's debt limit.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service RL31967, The Debt Limit: History and Recent Increases

facts.text: The first Liberty Loan of 1917 was oversubscribed by 50 percent, with more than four million subscribers.
facts.source: Federal Reserve History, Liberty Bonds

facts.text: About 20 million Americans bought Liberty Bonds in World War I, when the country had only 24 million households.
facts.source: Federal Reserve History, Liberty Bonds

facts.text: Roughly two-thirds of World War I funding came from bond sales and one-third from taxes.
facts.source: Federal Reserve History, Liberty Bonds

facts.text: Federal debt topped $25 billion by the end of 1919 as World War I bills came due.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: Budget surpluses in the 1920s cut the federal debt from about $24 billion to about $17 billion.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: By 1933 the federal deficit was nearly $3 billion and the debt had climbed past $22 billion.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: Treasury first offered U.S. Savings Bonds on March 1, 1935, and they later helped finance World War II.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: World War II cost an estimated $323 billion, and about $211 billion of it was borrowed.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: By the end of World War II, Savings Bonds made up almost 18 percent of the total public debt.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: Federal debt was about $259 billion on June 30, 1945, up from $43 billion five years earlier.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Historical Debt Outstanding

facts.text: Debt held by the public peaked at about 106 percent of GDP in 1946, right after World War II.
facts.source: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis: Gross Federal Debt Held by the Public as Percent of GDP
facts.note: FRED series FYPUGDA188S: 1946 = 106.31 percent, the maximum of the series (begins 1940).

facts.text: By 1974, debt held by the public was down to about 22 percent of GDP.
facts.source: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis: Gross Federal Debt Held by the Public as Percent of GDP
facts.note: FRED series FYPUGDA188S: 1974 = 22.24 percent.

facts.text: The federal government ran a budget surplus every year from 1946 through 1949.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: The 1969 federal budget surplus of $3.2 billion was the last one until 1998.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: In 1971, Treasury began selling notes by competitive auction, letting the market set interest rates.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: From 1980 to 1990, the national debt more than tripled as the government borrowed for military build-ups and new policies.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: The national debt was $998 billion at the end of fiscal 1981 and $1.14 trillion a year later.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Historical Debt Outstanding

facts.text: Treasury's daily data first showed more than $5 trillion of debt on February 23, 1996.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: First Debt to the Penny record with tot_pub_debt_out_amt of at least $5T is 1996-02-23 ($5.017T).

facts.text: Treasury's daily data first showed more than $10 trillion of debt on September 30, 2008.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: First record at or above $10T is 2008-09-30 ($10.025T); 2008-09-29 was $9.946T.

facts.text: Treasury's daily data first showed more than $15 trillion of debt on November 15, 2011.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: First record at or above $15T is 2011-11-15 ($15.034T).

facts.text: Treasury's daily data first showed more than $20 trillion of debt on September 8, 2017.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: First record at or above $20T is 2017-09-08 ($20.162T); 2017-09-07 was $19.845T.

facts.text: Treasury's daily data first showed more than $30 trillion of debt on January 31, 2022.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: First record at or above $30T is 2022-01-31 ($30.012T).

facts.text: Treasury's daily data first showed more than $40 trillion of debt on August 18, 2026.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: First record at or above $40T is 2026-08-18 ($40.047T); 2026-08-17 was $39.987T.

facts.text: It took nearly nine years for the debt to climb from $10 trillion to $20 trillion, from 2008 to 2017.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny

facts.text: The climb from $30 trillion to $40 trillion took about four and a half years, from January 2022 to August 2026.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny

facts.text: The most recent trillion came fast: debt went from $39 trillion on March 17, 2026 to $40 trillion on August 18.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: First record at or above $39T is 2026-03-17 ($39.017T); to 2026-08-18 is 154 days.

facts.text: The national debt grew by about $4.5 trillion in calendar year 2020, from $23.2 trillion to $27.7 trillion.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny

facts.text: The government ran four straight budget surpluses from fiscal 1998 to 2001, peaking at $236 billion in 2000.
facts.source: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis: Federal Surplus or Deficit

facts.text: The federal budget has run a deficit every year since its last surplus in 2001.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Understanding the National Deficit

facts.text: The federal deficit topped $1.4 trillion in fiscal 2009, during the Great Recession.
facts.source: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis: Federal Surplus or Deficit
facts.note: FRED series FYFSD: 2009 = -1,412,688 million.

facts.text: The federal deficit reached about $3.1 trillion in fiscal 2020 as the pandemic hit.
facts.source: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis: Federal Surplus or Deficit
facts.note: FRED series FYFSD: 2020 = -3,095,653 million.

facts.text: Gross federal debt passed 100 percent of GDP in 2013, when debt and GDP were each about $16.7 trillion.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Understanding the National Debt

facts.text: Federal spending rose about 50 percent from fiscal 2019 to fiscal 2021 in response to the pandemic.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Understanding the National Debt

facts.text: TreasuryDirect opened to the public in October 2002, first offering online Series I savings bonds.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: Debt held by the public has grown every year since 2001, Concord notes.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Thirty-three Years of Lessons Learned and What It Means for the Future

facts.text: As of October 9, 2026, the national debt was about $40.3 trillion.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny

facts.text: As of October 9, 2026, about $32.4 trillion of the debt was held by the public and $7.9 trillion by government accounts.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny
facts.note: debt_held_public_amt $32.448T; intragov_hold_amt $7.854T.

facts.text: In the 12 months to October 9, 2026, the national debt grew by about $2.4 trillion.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Debt to the Penny

facts.text: Treasury's Debt to the Penny dataset has daily national debt figures going back to April 1993.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Understanding the National Debt

facts.text: Debt held by the public is money owed to outsiders, such as investors, state governments, the Fed and foreign governments.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, FAQ

facts.text: Intragovernmental debt is what the government owes itself, mostly to trust funds like Social Security and Medicare.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, FAQ

facts.text: Treasury sells five kinds of marketable securities: bills, notes, bonds, inflation-protected securities and floating rate notes.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, About Treasury Marketable Securities

facts.text: Treasury bills mature in as little as 4 weeks or as long as 52 weeks.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, About Treasury Marketable Securities

facts.text: Treasury notes come in 2, 3, 5, 7 and 10 year terms and pay interest every six months.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, About Treasury Marketable Securities

facts.text: Treasury bonds are offered in 20 and 30 year terms and pay interest every six months.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, About Treasury Marketable Securities

facts.text: Inflation-protected Treasury securities, called TIPS, adjust their principal with the Consumer Price Index.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, About Treasury Marketable Securities

facts.text: Treasury floating rate notes last two years and pay interest quarterly, tied to 13-week bill rates.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, About Treasury Marketable Securities

facts.text: Treasury runs more than 425 debt auctions every year to fund the government.
facts.source: TreasuryDirect, The History of the Debt

facts.text: As of September 30, 2026, Treasury notes were the largest slice of marketable debt, at about $16.3 trillion.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Monthly Statement of the Public Debt Table 1 (September 2026)
facts.note: Notes total_mil_amt 16,281,507.

facts.text: As of September 30, 2026, about $7.1 trillion of the debt was in short-term Treasury bills.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Monthly Statement of the Public Debt Table 1 (September 2026)
facts.note: Bills total_mil_amt 7,118,145.

facts.text: On September 30, 2026, the average interest rate on all interest-bearing federal debt was 3.53 percent.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Average Interest Rates on Treasury Securities (September 2026)
facts.note: Total Interest-bearing Debt avg_interest_rate_amt = 3.531.

facts.text: Washington spent $7.0 trillion in fiscal 2025 but collected only $5.2 trillion in revenue.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Monthly Treasury Statement Table 9 (September 2025)
facts.note: Total outlays $7,009,973,667,049; total receipts $5,234,616,386,315 (fiscal year to date, September 2025).

facts.text: Social Security is the federal government's largest program, paying monthly benefits to over 71 million people in 2026.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service IF13256, Social Security: Selected Findings of the 2026 Annual Report (June 25, 2026)

facts.text: In 2026, about 186 million workers are covered by Social Security.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service IF13256, Social Security: Selected Findings of the 2026 Annual Report (June 25, 2026)

facts.text: Payroll taxes supplied 91.3 percent of Social Security's revenue in 2025.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service IF13256, Social Security: Selected Findings of the 2026 Annual Report (June 25, 2026)

facts.text: Social Security's trust fund reserves peaked at $2.91 trillion in 2020.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service IF13256, Social Security: Selected Findings of the 2026 Annual Report (June 25, 2026)

facts.text: The 2026 Trustees project Social Security's retirement fund runs dry in late 2032 and the combined funds in 2034.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service IF13256, Social Security: Selected Findings of the 2026 Annual Report (June 25, 2026)

facts.text: If Social Security's combined funds are depleted in 2034, tax income would cover about 83 percent of scheduled benefits.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service IF13256, Social Security: Selected Findings of the 2026 Annual Report (June 25, 2026)

facts.text: The 2026 Medicare Trustees Report projects the Hospital Insurance trust fund runs out in 2033, covering 89 percent of benefits.
facts.source: CMS, 2026 Annual Report of the Medicare Boards of Trustees

facts.text: In 1960 five workers paid taxes for each Social Security beneficiary; by 2025 the ratio was sinking below three to one.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Thirty-three Years of Lessons Learned and What It Means for the Future

facts.text: CBO's February 2026 baseline has debt held by the public reaching a record 120 percent of GDP by 2036.
facts.source: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, on CBO's February 2026 Budget and Economic Outlook

facts.text: CBO's February 2026 baseline has the annual deficit growing to $3.1 trillion by 2036.
facts.source: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, on CBO's February 2026 Budget and Economic Outlook

facts.text: CBO projects Social Security and health care spending will grow from 11.2 percent of GDP in 2025 to 12.5 percent in 2036.
facts.source: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, on CBO's February 2026 Budget and Economic Outlook

facts.text: Concord Action reports private investors held roughly 60 percent of Treasuries in September 2026, up from 37 percent in 2014.
facts.source: Concord Action, The New Buyers of U.S. Debt (Sept 30, 2026)

facts.text: Foreign governments held 34 percent of publicly held Treasuries in 2014 and about 17 percent by September 2026, Concord Action reports.
facts.source: Concord Action, The New Buyers of U.S. Debt (Sept 30, 2026)

facts.text: Hedge funds roughly doubled their Treasury exposure to about $4 trillion between 2023 and September 2025.
facts.source: Concord Action, The New Buyers of U.S. Debt (Sept 30, 2026)

facts.text: The Federal Reserve held about $4.8 trillion of federal debt at the end of June 2026, down from a $6.3 trillion peak in early 2022.
facts.source: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis: Federal Debt Held by Federal Reserve Banks
facts.note: FRED FDHBFRBN: 2026 Q2 = 4,780.1 billion; max 6,254.966 billion in 2022 Q1 (end of period).

facts.text: Foreign and international investors held about $9.4 trillion of federal debt at the end of March 2026.
facts.source: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis: Federal Debt Held by Foreign and International Investors
facts.note: FRED FDHBFIN: 2026 Q1 = 9,355.0 billion (end of period).

facts.text: Gross federal debt equaled about 123 percent of GDP in the first quarter of 2026.
facts.source: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis: Total Public Debt as Percent of GDP
facts.note: FRED GFDEGDQ188S: 2026 Q1 = 122.59 percent.

facts.text: Mandatory spending, which needs no annual vote in Congress, makes up nearly two-thirds of federal spending.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Federal Spending

facts.text: CBO estimated the federal deficit at about $2.0 trillion through the first 11 months of fiscal 2026.
facts.source: Concord Action, The New Fiscal Year Begins With $40 Trillion Debt (Oct 1, 2026)

facts.text: The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget estimates debt held by the public ended fiscal 2026 near 100 percent of GDP.
facts.source: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, FY 2026 deficit estimate (Oct 1, 2026)

facts.text: In fiscal 2025, net interest of $970 billion topped national defense spending of $917 billion.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Monthly Treasury Statement Table 9 (September 2025)
facts.note: Net Interest $970,358,886,994; National Defense $916,648,676,662.

facts.text: The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget estimates fiscal 2026 interest costs hit a record $1.1 trillion.
facts.source: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, FY 2026 deficit estimate (Oct 1, 2026)

facts.text: In October 2026, Concord Action said net interest consumes over 20 percent of federal tax dollars.
facts.source: Concord Action, Another Fiscal Year, Another $2 Trillion Hole (Oct 8, 2026)

facts.text: Concord reported in 2025 that interest as a share of federal revenue more than doubled in a decade, from 7 to nearly 20 percent.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Thirty-three Years of Lessons Learned and What It Means for the Future

facts.text: CBO projects net interest will reach $2.1 trillion a year by 2036, up from $970 billion in 2025.
facts.source: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, on CBO's February 2026 Budget and Economic Outlook

facts.text: On September 30, 2026, the 10-year Treasury yield rose above 5.30 percent, a 24-year high, Concord Action reports.
facts.source: Concord Action, The New Fiscal Year Begins With $40 Trillion Debt (Oct 1, 2026)

facts.text: If rates average 1.5 points above projections, CBO estimates deficits would grow by $6 trillion through 2036.
facts.source: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, on CBO's interest-rate analysis (Oct 8, 2026)

facts.text: Interest costs are now more than triple the $350 billion a year paid between 2018 and 2021, one budget watchdog estimates.
facts.source: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, FY 2026 deficit estimate (Oct 1, 2026)

facts.text: Kitty Kurth recalls Tsongas wanted less spent on interest so money remained for education and other priorities.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Facing the Future: The 1992 Tsongas Campaign and the Birth of The Concord Coalition (Jan 6, 2022)

facts.text: The Budget and Accounting Act of 1921 required the President to submit an annual budget to Congress.
facts.source: U.S. House of Representatives, History, Art & Archives: Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974

facts.text: The Budget Act signed July 12, 1974 created the House and Senate Budget Committees and the nonpartisan CBO.
facts.source: U.S. House of Representatives, History, Art & Archives: Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974

facts.text: The 1974 Budget Act moved the start of the federal fiscal year from July 1 to October 1.
facts.source: U.S. House of Representatives, History, Art & Archives: Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974

facts.text: The 1974 Budget Act also created reconciliation, a fast-track tool for passing budget legislation.
facts.source: U.S. House of Representatives, History, Art & Archives: Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974

facts.text: A 1972 debt limit bill created the study committee that designed the 1974 congressional budget process.
facts.source: U.S. Senate Committee on the Budget, Committee History

facts.text: In 1972, automatic Social Security cost-of-living increases passed as an amendment to a debt limit bill.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, History and Future of the Social Security Trust Fund: Part II (Aug 23, 2023)

facts.text: Gramm-Rudman-Hollings, signed December 12, 1985, set annual deficit targets that fell to zero by fiscal 1991.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R41901, Statutory Budget Controls in Effect Between 1985 and 2002

facts.text: The 1985 deficit-target law rode along on a bill raising the debt limit to $2.079 trillion.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R41901, Statutory Budget Controls in Effect Between 1985 and 2002

facts.text: In July 1986, the Supreme Court struck down Gramm-Rudman-Hollings' automatic cut mechanism in Bowsher v. Synar.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R41901, Statutory Budget Controls in Effect Between 1985 and 2002

facts.text: The Budget Enforcement Act, signed November 5, 1990, introduced PAYGO rules and caps on discretionary spending.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R41901, Statutory Budget Controls in Effect Between 1985 and 2002

facts.text: A fall 1990 budget summit at Andrews Air Force Base produced a five-year, $500 billion deficit reduction plan.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R41901, Statutory Budget Controls in Effect Between 1985 and 2002

facts.text: The Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act, signed February 12, 2010, is meant to keep new tax and mandatory spending laws budget neutral.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R41157, The Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act of 2010

facts.text: The 2010 statutory PAYGO law was attached to a bill raising the debt limit to $14.294 trillion.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R41157, The Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act of 2010

facts.text: The Budget Control Act, signed August 2, 2011, capped discretionary spending, which CBO estimated would save $917 billion.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R41965, The Budget Control Act of 2011

facts.text: If the 2011 Joint Select Committee missed its $1.2 trillion deficit goal, automatic cuts called sequestration would follow.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R41965, The Budget Control Act of 2011

facts.text: The Budget Act sets April 15 for adopting a budget resolution, but Congress has met that date only four times since FY1986.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R47235, The Congressional Budget Process Timeline (July 29, 2025)

facts.text: Congress adopted no budget resolution in 13 of the 50 fiscal years since the first one for fiscal 1976.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R47235, The Congressional Budget Process Timeline (July 29, 2025)

facts.text: A budget resolution is passed by the House and Senate but never signed by the President, and it is not a law.
facts.source: U.S. Senate Committee on the Budget, Committee History

facts.text: Fiscal 1997 was the last time Congress enacted all of its regular spending bills by the October 1 start of the year.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service IN12324, Omnibus Appropriations: Overview of Recent Practice

facts.text: From fiscal 1997 through 2025, only 25 of 330 regular appropriations acts were enacted by October 1.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R47235, The Congressional Budget Process Timeline (July 29, 2025)

facts.text: House and Senate Appropriations each have 12 subcommittees, one for every regular spending bill.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R47106, The Appropriations Process: A Brief Overview

facts.text: A continuing resolution keeps agencies funded for a short time when regular spending bills are not done by October 1.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R47235, The Congressional Budget Process Timeline (July 29, 2025)

facts.text: By law the President's budget is due on the first Monday in February, eight months before the fiscal year starts.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R47235, The Congressional Budget Process Timeline (July 29, 2025)
facts.note: Budget due first Monday in February; fiscal year begins October 1. 'Eight months' is approximate (about 8 months).

facts.text: The longest government shutdown ran from October 1 to November 12, 2025, lasting 42 full days.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R41759, Past Government Shutdowns: Key Resources (updated Sept 16, 2026)

facts.text: The previous record shutdown, which began in December 2018, lasted 34 full days.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R41759, Past Government Shutdowns: Key Resources (updated Sept 16, 2026)

facts.text: The debt limit is $41.1 trillion, set by a $5.0 trillion increase in July 2025.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service IF10292, The Debt Limit (updated Sept 21, 2026)

facts.text: Congress has approved 104 separate debt limit changes since the end of World War II.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service IF10292, The Debt Limit (updated Sept 21, 2026)

facts.text: Congress has made 22 distinct changes to the debt limit since 2001.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service IF10292, The Debt Limit (updated Sept 21, 2026)

facts.text: In July 1939, Congress set the first single debt limit covering nearly all public debt, at $45 billion.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service RL31967, The Debt Limit: History and Recent Increases

facts.text: Debt subject to the debt limit is more than 99 percent of all federal debt.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service IF10292, The Debt Limit (updated Sept 21, 2026)

facts.text: Article I of the Constitution gives Congress the power to borrow money on the credit of the United States.
facts.source: National Archives, The Constitution of the United States: A Transcription

facts.text: The Constitution says no money may leave the Treasury except through appropriations made by law.
facts.source: National Archives, The Constitution of the United States: A Transcription

facts.text: The Constitution requires a regular public statement of the government's receipts and expenditures.
facts.source: National Archives, The Constitution of the United States: A Transcription

facts.text: The Constitution says all bills for raising revenue must originate in the House of Representatives.
facts.source: National Archives, The Constitution of the United States: A Transcription

facts.text: Section 4 of the 14th Amendment says the validity of the public debt of the United States shall not be questioned.
facts.source: National Archives, Constitution Amendments 11-27

facts.text: The United States has never defaulted on its obligations, according to Treasury's Fiscal Data.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Understanding the National Debt

facts.text: The federal fiscal year runs from October 1 through September 30.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, FAQ

facts.text: A deficit is one year's gap between spending and revenue, and the debt is the total of those past gaps.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, FAQ

facts.text: Discretionary spending is set in annual appropriations, while mandatory spending follows laws already on the books.
facts.source: U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data, Federal Spending

facts.text: The Concord Coalition was founded in September 1992 to build a grassroots movement for fiscal responsibility.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Thirty-three Years of Lessons Learned and What It Means for the Future

facts.text: Concord's founders were former Senators Paul Tsongas and Warren Rudman and former Commerce Secretary Peter G. Peterson.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition (archived site), About Us

facts.text: Concord is named for the 1775 stand at Concord, Massachusetts, where farmers called Minutemen turned back British soldiers.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition (archived site), About Us

facts.text: Paul Tsongas liked to point to Paul Revere, who got on his horse instead of ringing his bell from home.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Facing the Future: The 1992 Tsongas Campaign and the Birth of The Concord Coalition (Jan 6, 2022)
facts.note: Quote is from Concord national field director Phil Smith recalling Tsongas.

facts.text: Concord's first staffer, Kitty Kurth, helped set up a field network in all 50 states within six weeks.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Facing the Future: The 1992 Tsongas Campaign and the Birth of The Concord Coalition (Jan 6, 2022)

facts.text: Paul Tsongas won the 1992 New Hampshire primary, then helped launch The Concord Coalition that same year.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Facing the Future: The 1992 Tsongas Campaign and the Birth of The Concord Coalition (Jan 6, 2022)

facts.text: Concord's mission is to educate, engage and empower citizens with credible, nonpartisan information about federal debt.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Who We Are

facts.text: Concord organizes citizens to act on the debt without regard to party affiliation.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition (archived site), About Us

facts.text: The Concord Coalition is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, and Concord Action is a separate 501(c)(4) advocacy organization.
facts.source: Concord Action, Who We Are
facts.note: Stated in the footer banners of concordcoalition.org and concordaction.org.

facts.text: Dr. Carolyn Bourdeaux is executive director of both The Concord Coalition and Concord Action.
facts.source: Concord Action, Who We Are

facts.text: Before joining Concord, Dr. Bourdeaux served in Congress from Georgia in 2021 and 2022.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Who We Are

facts.text: Dr. Bourdeaux once directed Georgia's Senate Budget and Evaluation Office during the Great Recession.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Who We Are

facts.text: Concord's board is co-chaired by former Senators John Danforth and Bob Kerrey.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Who We Are
facts.note: Who We Are lists Danforth and Kerrey as Co-Chairs; archived About Us calls them former Senators.

facts.text: In Concord's Principles & Priorities, groups of five to ten step into Congress's shoes to see how hard balancing the budget is.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Principles & Priorities

facts.text: Concord's Principles & Priorities exercise can run for as few as 8 people or as many as 200.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Principles & Priorities

facts.text: In Concord's Penny Game, one penny stands for 1 percent of federal spending, about $70 billion in fiscal 2025.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, The Penny Game

facts.text: To show the deficit, Concord's Penny Game covers 25 of 100 pennies in red tape to mean borrowed money.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, The Penny Game

facts.text: Concord's Chart Talk presentation walks through what is driving the national debt and why it matters.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Budget Exercises

facts.text: Concord's weekly radio show and podcast, Facing the Future, is hosted by Robert Bixby.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Who We Are
facts.note: Who We Are says Bixby hosts the weekly podcast; Concord's Jan 6, 2022 post is written in his voice as host.

facts.text: Robert Bixby joined Concord in 1992 and became its executive director in 1999.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Who We Are

facts.text: Concord's Fiscal Wake-Up Tour was featured in the documentary film I.O.U.S.A.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Who We Are

facts.text: Concord's September 2026 North Carolina Debt Clock Tour was set to visit NC State, Duke and UNC Chapel Hill.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Concord Coalition Brings $40 Trillion Debt Warning to Raleigh (Sept 18, 2026)

facts.text: Fiscal Lookouts are Concord's volunteer super advocates who meet members of Congress and organize local events.
facts.source: Concord Action, Volunteer

facts.text: The 2027 National Citizens Debt Summit is March 2 to 4, 2027, at the Hilton Washington D.C. Capitol Hill.
facts.source: Concord Action, 2027 National Citizens Debt Summit

facts.text: Summit attendees will meet with their member of Congress and key Washington decision-makers.
facts.source: Concord Action, 2027 National Citizens Debt Summit

facts.text: Concord Action's top advocates gathered in Washington for a Debt Summit on June 3, 2026.
facts.source: Concord Action, Events
facts.note: Events page title: 2026 Concord Citizen Volunteer Debt Summit. Volunteer page calls it the inaugural Debt Summit.

facts.text: Concord Action says it has grown by over 200,000 citizen activists in the past year, as of October 2026.
facts.source: Concord Action, Another Fiscal Year, Another $2 Trillion Hole (Oct 8, 2026)

facts.text: An August 2026 Concord Action town hall had experts from Cato and Brookings debate Social Security's future.
facts.source: Concord Action, Events

facts.text: The 1994 Kerrey-Danforth Commission had 30 of its 32 members agree on seven findings about the nation's finances.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Kerrey-Danforth Commission Findings Still Need Solutions Thirty Years Later

facts.text: Concord co-founder Warren Rudman was also a Senate sponsor of the 1985 Gramm-Rudman-Hollings deficit law.
facts.source: Congressional Research Service R41901, Statutory Budget Controls in Effect Between 1985 and 2002
facts.note: CRS R41901 names Senators Gramm, Rudman and Hollings as sponsors; Rudman's role as Concord co-founder is from https://archive.concordcoalition.org/about-us/.

facts.text: Concord notes the federal budget has no line item labeled waste, fraud, and abuse.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Thirty-three Years of Lessons Learned and What It Means for the Future

facts.text: For its 30th anniversary in 2022, Concord planned to take its budget exercise to 30 college campuses.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Facing the Future: The 1992 Tsongas Campaign and the Birth of The Concord Coalition (Jan 6, 2022)

facts.text: Concord calls CBO's projections the closest thing to a common set of facts for policy debates.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Thirty-three Years of Lessons Learned and What It Means for the Future

facts.text: Concord Action backs the bipartisan 3% Resolution, which aims to cut the deficit in half.
facts.source: Concord Action, Cut the Debt Campaign

facts.text: Concord Action's No Budget, No Pay campaign says Congress should go unpaid if it misses a budget.
facts.source: Concord Action, Cut the Debt Campaign

facts.text: Since Concord's founding in 1992, real economic growth has topped 5 percent only once and averaged 2.6 percent a year.
facts.source: The Concord Coalition, Thirty-three Years of Lessons Learned and What It Means for the Future
